questions.question: What is the difference between buffered and unbuffered channels in Go?
questions.title: Buffered and unbuffered channel semantics
questions.direct_answer: An unbuffered channel has capacity zero, so a send completes only when a receiver is ready to take that value. A buffered channel holds up to its capacity, so sends can complete while space exists and receives can complete while data exists. A buffer changes synchronization and backpressure; it does not make communication asynchronous or remove blocking.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the readiness and synchronization rules rather than only channel creation syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying a buffered channel never blocks or adding a large buffer to hide a stuck consumer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the handoff, queue, and happens-before consequences of capacity.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Unbuffered means capacity zero and a direct sender-receiver handoff.
A buffered send can proceed only while the queue has space.
A buffered receive can proceed only while the queue has data, unless the channel is closed.
Both channel kinds can block and synchronize goroutines.
Capacity is part of the concurrency contract, not a universal speed setting.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An unbuffered channel has no queue. A sender and receiver must meet for one value to cross, so the send cannot complete until a receiver has accepted that value. This gives a strong handoff point between the two goroutines.

A buffered channel has a fixed queue. A send can complete when there is an empty slot, even if no receiver is ready at that moment. A receive can complete when an item is already queued. Once the buffer is full, another send blocks; once it is empty, another receive blocks.

For example, `make(chan string, 2)` lets a producer place two jobs before it must wait for the consumer. That can absorb a small, expected burst, but it does not fix a consumer that never runs. An unbuffered version instead applies backpressure on every job and confirms each handoff.

I choose based on the required coordination. I use unbuffered communication when the handoff itself matters, and a measured buffer when bounded decoupling is part of the design. Neither choice protects unrelated shared variables, and neither should be used to guess around a deadlock.

sections.title: Capacity moves the wait point
sections.content:
With capacity zero, there is no intermediate owner: sender and receiver synchronize on each transfer. With capacity greater than zero, the channel queue temporarily owns sent values. The producer waits later—when every slot is occupied—while the consumer waits when no value is queued.

That shift affects ordering guarantees. A send is synchronized before the receive that obtains its value. The memory model also relates buffered receives and later sends through the channel capacity. The safe rule is to use channel operations as the synchronization boundary and never infer visibility merely because a goroutine probably ran during an available buffer slot.

sections.title: Where communication waits
sections.content:
| Situation | Unbuffered `make(chan T)` | Buffered `make(chan T, 2)` |
|---|---|---|
| Sender, no receiver | Waits | Queues until 2 slots fill |
| Receiver, no value | Waits | Waits when queue is empty |
| Transfer meaning | Direct handoff | Ownership moves through queue |
| Backpressure | Every transfer | When capacity is exhausted |
| Useful for | Rendezvous and exact handoff | Bounded bursts and bounded queues |

sections.title: Observe the buffer boundary
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    jobs := make(chan string, 2)
    jobs <- "compile"
    jobs <- "test"

    fmt.Println(len(jobs), cap(jobs))
    fmt.Println(<-jobs)
    fmt.Println(<-jobs)
}
```
Both sends complete because two slots exist. The output is `2 2`, then `compile`, then `test`; one sender preserves FIFO order.

questions.question: How should you choose the capacity of a buffered Go channel?
questions.title: Choosing a channel buffer capacity
questions.direct_answer: Choose channel capacity from a bounded requirement: the burst you intentionally absorb, the number of permits you expose, or the exact in-flight work the protocol allows. Capacity one is useful for a single result that must not strand its sender. Avoid arbitrary large buffers; they postpone backpressure, retain memory, and can hide lifecycle bugs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether buffer size is derived from a protocol or resource budget instead of folklore.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Increasing capacity until a timing-dependent test passes without fixing ownership or cancellation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name queueing latency, memory retention, and backpressure as observable consequences.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Capacity should represent a known burst, permit count, or in-flight limit.
A one-result channel can let a worker report even if the caller takes another path.
A larger queue delays producer backpressure and can increase latency and memory use.
A buffer cannot repair a missing receiver, forgotten close, or absent cancellation path.
Measure queue depth and processing rate when capacity affects production behaviour.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I treat channel capacity as part of the protocol. It should answer a concrete question such as “how many burst items may wait,” “how many operations may be active,” or “how many results can arrive before collection begins.” If there is no such requirement, an unbuffered channel gives the simplest backpressure.

Capacity one is common for a single-result operation. A worker can send one result and finish even if the caller is simultaneously selecting cancellation. For a job queue, the capacity may match a small accepted burst, but worker count—not queue size—normally controls how many external calls run at once.

For example, a two-worker service might accept four queued jobs because the product allows a short burst of six in-flight requests: two processing and four waiting. Beyond that, producers block or the API explicitly rejects work. That is a business and resource decision, not a magic Go number.

Oversizing trades visible pressure for hidden backlog. Queued values retain memory and may become stale while waiting. I monitor depth and wait time, test saturation and cancellation, and change capacity only with evidence. If enlarging a buffer merely makes a deadlock disappear, the lifecycle is still wrong.

sections.title: A buffer is a bounded ownership queue
sections.content:
A queued value has left the producer but has not reached the consumer. The channel temporarily owns it, along with any memory reachable from it. More capacity therefore means more work can be accepted without proof that downstream can keep up. This can be useful for short bursts, but under sustained overload the buffer eventually fills and latency grows before backpressure becomes visible.

Some capacities encode a stronger invariant. A capacity-three token channel can represent three permits. A result channel with capacity equal to the number of workers can ensure each worker can publish one terminal result. These sizes can be explained and tested. “Large enough not to block” cannot, because real load can always exceed the guess.

sections.title: Derive capacity from a requirement
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Need a channel] --> B{Must sender meet receiver now?}
  B -- Yes --> U[Capacity 0]
  B -- No --> C{Known burst, permits, or result count?}
  C -- No --> R[Recheck protocol and ownership]
  C -- Yes --> D[Set bounded capacity]
  D --> E[Test full queue, cancellation, memory]
  E --> F[Observe depth and wait time]
```

sections.title: Use capacity one for one terminal result
